metadata.title: Explaining the gender gaps in mathematics achievement and attitudes_ The role of societal gender equality

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA’s stratified two-stage sampling design (schools sampled first, then students randomly selected within schools) and applies the final student weights that incorporate both school weights and within-school student weights. For the 2012 analysis, the authors explicitly state that they use final student weights in the econometric stage. For the cross-country panel regressions, they additionally estimate country-level weights inversely proportional to the estimated standard error of the unexplained gap from the decomposition stage. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) for the panel regressions, but it does use bootstrap replications to obtain standard errors for decomposition components.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that PISA plausible values are averaged to form test score measures (e.g., “average of the five plausible values”), but it does not provide a complete, explicit missing-data handling rule for all variables used in the propensity score estimation and decomposition. It does mention severe missingness for the self-concept index and that they exclude it from the analysis, but the overall missing-data strategy for the remaining covariates is not fully documented. This is a reporting gap because missingness can affect propensity score overlap and the decomposition estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The main decomposition for math achievement and math attitudes is based on the 2012 PISA sample restricted to 56 countries/economies for which societal gender equity indicators (GGI and/or domain-specific labor-market indicators) are available. The authors use the 2012 PISA target population of 15-year-olds enrolled in grade 7 or above and apply PISA final student weights (school + within-school). For math attitudes, they use only the self-efficacy index and the intrinsic/instrumental motivation indices; they explicitly do not use the self-concept index due to severe missingness. In the semiparametric Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition, they further restrict the estimation to the common support subpopulation defined by overlap in estimated propensity scores between females and males, discarding observations outside the overlap region. For panel analyses, they pool 2006, 2009, 2012, and 2015 waves for math and reading gaps, but restrict attitude analyses to 2012 because attitude measures are not available in other waves.

main_findings.target_variable: Unexplained part of mean gender gap in mathematics achievement
main_findings.performance_metrics: Semiparametric Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (2012 PISA): unexplained component statistically significant in 53/56 countries; boys advantage in unexplained part ranges from 35.97 score points (Czech Republic) to 5.11 score points (Russia).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged gender and observable student/family characteristics (grade level, parental education and occupation, books, and home educational resources) to decompose the gender gap into explained and unexplained parts, finding that the unexplained component of the mean gender gap in mathematics achievement is statistically significant in most countries and favors boys. This indicates that differences in observed inputs do not fully account for the gender math achievement gap, so policy should also target mechanisms beyond measurable student background (e.g., school processes and gendered expectations), while causality cannot be inferred from the descriptive cross-country associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; math self-efficacy, PV-averaged index)
main_findings.target_variable: Unexplained part of mean gender gap in mathematics self-efficacy
main_findings.performance_metrics: Semiparametric Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (2012 PISA): gender gap in self-efficacy statistically significant in 53/56 countries; unexplained part statistically significant in all countries and favors boys; unexplained part varies from 0.07 units (Malaysia) to 0.66 units (Germany).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged gender and observable student/family characteristics to decompose the gender gap in mathematics self-efficacy into explained and unexplained components, finding that the unexplained component is statistically significant in all countries and favors boys. This indicates that even after accounting for observable differences, gendered factors associated with confidence in math remain, suggesting that interventions should focus on reducing gender-specific barriers to math self-beliefs (e.g., feedback practices and stereotype-related mechanisms), though the study does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; intrinsic motivation to learn math index)
main_findings.target_variable: Unexplained part of mean gender gap in intrinsic motivation to learn mathematics
main_findings.performance_metrics: Semiparametric Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (2012 PISA): gender gap in intrinsic motivation statistically significant in 49/56 countries; unexplained part statistically significant in 49 countries and favors boys; unexplained part ranges from 0.07 units (Bulgaria) to 0.45 units (Switzerland); Malaysia is the only country where unexplained part favors girls.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged gender and observable characteristics to decompose the gender gap in intrinsic motivation to learn math, finding that the unexplained component is statistically significant in most countries and generally favors boys. This indicates that gender differences in intrinsic motivation are not fully explained by measured student and family inputs, so practice should consider gender-responsive motivational supports and classroom climate factors beyond socioeconomic composition, while causality remains untested.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; instrumental motivation to learn math index)
main_findings.target_variable: Unexplained part of mean gender gap in instrumental motivation to learn mathematics
main_findings.performance_metrics: Semiparametric Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (2012 PISA): gender gap in instrumental motivation statistically significant in most countries (Table 4); explained part statistically significant in 7 countries (mostly favoring boys); unexplained part statistically insignificant in 16 countries and otherwise favors boys.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged gender and observable characteristics to decompose the gender gap in instrumental motivation to learn math, finding that the unexplained component is often statistically significant and typically favors boys. This indicates that gendered perceptions of the usefulness of math for future careers persist beyond measured background differences, implying that career-linked math messaging and guidance may need to be gender-sensitive, though the analysis is descriptive rather than causal.

main_findings.target_variable: Unexplained part of mean gender gap in reading achievement
main_findings.performance_metrics: Semiparametric Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (2012 PISA): girls outperform boys in reading in all 56 countries; unexplained part is in favor of girls and statistically significant in all countries; unexplained part varies from 11.12 score points (Belgium) to 49.08 score points (Finland).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Reading the study leveraged gender and observable characteristics to decompose the gender gap into explained and unexplained parts, finding that the unexplained component consistently favors girls and is statistically significant in all countries. This indicates that gendered factors affecting achievement differ by domain (reading vs math), so education policy should avoid one-size-fits-all gender gap interventions and instead tailor supports to domain-specific mechanisms.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2006/2009/2012/2015 Mathematics (panel; unexplained gap as DV)
main_findings.target_variable: Association between societal gender equity and unexplained gender gap in mathematics achievement
top_predictors: Gender equity in tertiary education access
main_findings.performance_metrics: Cross-country panel regressions (Eq. 11; Table 7): GGI coefficient not significant; gender equity in access to tertiary education and lower gender wage gap significantly predict a smaller unexplained part of the gender math gap favoring boys. Table 7 also reports that GDP per capita and the female-to-male ratio among test-takers are not statistically significant in the preferred specification.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using pooled PISA waves (2006, 2009, 2012, 2015) for mathematics, the study leveraged country-level gender equity measures (especially tertiary education access and wage equality) to explain variation in the unexplained component of the gender math gap, finding that these societal equity domains are significantly associated with a smaller boys-favoring unexplained gap. This indicates that policy efforts targeting women’s access to higher education and reducing gender wage inequality may help narrow the gender math achievement gap beyond individual-level composition, though the authors explicitly avoid causal claims due to endogeneity concerns.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA microdata to explain cross-country gender gaps in mathematics achievement and mathematics-related attitudes through a two-stage semiparametric Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition. For the first stage, it analyzes the 2012 PISA mathematics domain (and 2012 reading for heterogeneity) using PV-averaged test scores and decomposes each country’s mean gender gap into an explained part (accounting for observable student/family characteristics and school fixed effects) and an unexplained part. The unexplained component is statistically significant in most countries for math achievement and math attitudes, generally favoring boys, while reading gaps favor girls in all countries. In the second stage, the authors relate the unexplained components to societal gender equity measures (GGI and domain-specific indicators) using pooled panel data across 2006, 2009, 2012, and 2015 waves for math and reading. They find that composite GGI is not significant, but gender equity in tertiary education access and wage equality significantly predicts a smaller boys-favoring unexplained math gap. Limitations include descriptive (non-causal) interpretation due to potential omitted-variable bias and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling beyond the self-concept index.
